/method/.title: Method — The Luwinski Archive
blocks: what the labels mean, and who is missing
every claim here carries a confidence and a source. the point of labelling is that a reader can overturn the reasoning without having to take the conclusion on trust.
¦documented a named source with a reference, and where possible the scan. the gedenkbuch entries, the marriage certificate number, the deportation dates.

¦inferred a reasoned conclusion from documented facts, with the reasoning written out so it can be attacked. the paternity finding is here. it stayed here through the y-dna result of 14 september 2026 — which corroborated it rather than overturning it — because a conclusion does not become documented by surviving a test. it becomes documented when there is a document.
¦disputed asserted in the family record and contradicted by what can be seen. georg leibholz as a brother; the february 1948 marriage date.
¦unproven kept because it may matter later, but carrying no weight now. the hundred-odd surname-index luwinskis.

a living person (80 or younger, with no death recorded) is named with their relationships and their town and country, and nothing more. no date of any kind — not a birth year, not a marriage or a divorce — no record, no source, no photograph, no cause of death and no structured data. 4 people are published on that footing, and every one has a page of their own, as does every other person in the register.

a living person’s page is noindex, which takes it out of the sitemap and out of this site’s search, and it carries no table, no image and no year. they are also named in the blood-relatives chart and in the family drawn on a relative’s page. the town and country are the place of birth where the family tree records one for them, and are left blank where it records none, or records only a street address or an institution. 0 have a town and a country, 1 a country only and 3 no place.

who is living is decided by one definition, shared by every archive in this estate (living_rule.py in the kit), and not by a test of this archive’s own: born 80 years ago or less, by year, with no death or burial recorded (dated or not) and no public record source. a person with no birth year cannot be shown to be that young, so is not living; a person the tree flags as possibly alive but who is older than that, or whose birth year is not known, is published as not living, with the absence of a death record stated plainly. several of those are holocaust-era people whose fate was never recorded. saying so is the entry’s purpose.

a person who might be a child is not published at all — no record, no page, not even as someone’s relative. that is anyone not recorded dead, with no public source and no birth year, who has a living parent. a child whose birth year is known is not held out: they are living, and are shown as a living person is. it is computed from the tree, not listed by hand.

the rule is applied where the register is generated, not in the templates, so a living person’s dates never reach a committed file. check:living then tests the built pages against it, and recomputes who is living from the private tree by the kit’s rule without asking the generator: it fails if anything beyond a name, a relationship and a town and country is found with a living person’s name, if the generated register carries a field it should not, if a living person’s page can be indexed, has structured data, a table, an image or a year, if a person who is held out appears anywhere, or if anyone the archive names has no page.

one exception, and it goes the other way. lynn derrick luwinski is named, with his parents, and nothing else — no occupation, no address, not even a town, no photograph, no descendants. an archive about a man’s ancestry that would not say whose ancestry it was would be useless; an archive that published him would be a different kind of failure.
a removal request is honoured within days, without argument and without requiring a reason.
a plausible number from a check that could not see the thing 21 september 2026

the worst failure this archive meets is not an error. it is a reasonable-looking answer about the wrong object, because nothing about it asks to be checked. six instances landed in a single day, four of them inside an hour, and they share one shape: a test ran, found nothing, and reported the nothing as a fact about the world rather than a fact about itself.

the scan that stopped before the name. the le‑ block was measured on schöneberg's registers and carried to kreuzberg's without rechecking. kreuzberg 1980 reported no leipholz with its last word at leipelt, and 1981 with its last at leimbach — both of which sort before the name being looked for. the scan had never reached it.
the volume with two alphabets. kreuzberg 1982 is 226 pages where its neighbours are 125, and holds two registers. reading it as one sequence covers half the year and calls the whole of it empty.

the spelling the search could not contain. a scan for leibholz read the 1975 schöneberg index and declared it clean. widening the pattern to le[iy][bp]h found erna frida else leipholz in the same volume on the first pass.
the surname settled by its neighbours. a telephone book prints “leibholz erna”. she is a leipholz, and no better scan shows it — the line sits between leipert and leipner, where leibholz cannot be.

the dates that were there all along. a visiting session reported this archive's atlas as carrying no dates. it has no date key; fifteen of its sixteen places carry a year in prose. the check looked for a field and reported a world.
the index nobody fetched. the search page fetched a file that existed only between builds. every gate passed, because no gate opened what the page asks for.

the rule that comes out of it is not “be careful”. it is that a negative must carry proof that the instrument reached the place. this archive now requires a scan to return the nearest name on each side of the target, and treats a result with an empty side as inconclusive rather than negative. a gate must derive what to check from what the page actually asks for, not from a list somebody maintains. and when several negatives share a property — an umlaut, a suffix, a blank parameter, a spelling — suspect the property before believing any of them.
it is the tidy negative that should frighten us 21 september 2026

a sister archive spent an afternoon on record searches that returned zero, and was one step from publishing a finding that explained all of its evidence and was built on nothing. its own summary of what went wrong is better than the incident: noise looks like noise; it is the tidy negative that should frighten us.
three failures here the same week had that same shape, and none of them looked like an error:
a clean year-by-year scan of the 1942 death index, reporting no leibholz. the volume has no text layer at all. the search was matching against an empty string and returning a tidy, orderly nothing.
four complete-looking register pages. the browser pane had quietly resized, so each page was captured half-height. a cropped page of a ruled table is indistinguishable from a whole one.
a scan that stopped before the name. it reported an absence at kreuzberg 1980 with its last surname at leipelt — which sorts before the name being looked for.

every one produced a result with internal structure. that is the tell, and it is the opposite of the intuition: a garbled answer gets checked, a neat one gets published. in each case the instrument was describing itself while appearing to describe the world.

and a healthy neighbour proves nothing. throughout that archive's dead afternoon the image host kept serving plates perfectly, in the same browser. a day of successful image reads is not evidence that the search beside it is alive. here, the zlb page images and the zlb text index are likewise separate instruments and can fail apart.

the cause turned out to be narrower than first reported and the correction is worth keeping too: the account was never signed out, one browser context was, and it recovered on its own. each session holds its own cookies, so a probe run from a different session would have come back clean and proved nothing. a check on a shared service has to run in the same context as the work it is vouching for.
the decisive fact was in a third file 21 september 2026
two sessions worked on this archive on the same morning and both got georg leibholz wrong, in opposite directions, within an hour of each other.

a visiting session read the status field — documented — but not a brother — and rendered exactly that. it was accurate when written and it is a summary of research at a moment, so the page stated the half that was in the data. this archive then corrected it with the newer finding: sally leibholz, father of the three, was also born at hammerstein, so a hammerstein birth no longer puts a man outside this family — and wrote that the reason for expecting georg to be separate had gone.

that was wrong too, and this archive's own atlas said so. the hammerstein pin reads “georg born 1884 — which is why he cannot be jacob's brother.” georg was born 7 june 1884 and jacob on 8 august 1884, two months apart, and two men born two months apart are not brothers. the point survives the one-year discrepancy in georg's record, because 7 june 1885 still leaves ten months. he is excluded by calculation, which is a stronger and more final thing than an absence of proof: an absence invites somebody to go looking, a calculation closes it.

a visiting session reads the summary. a resident session reads the moment it happens to remember. the fact that settled it was in a third file that neither had opened. the resident failure is the worse of the two, because it was committed while explaining the visitor's.
the gate watched the pages and not the data widened, 20 september 2026

check:living exists so that the promise about living people is tested against the built output rather than trusted to the generator. until tonight it walked *.html only — and this site serves two json files that a reader's browser fetches directly: the atlas data behind the map, and the search index. a living person could have reached a reader through either without the build saying a word.

a peer session working across the shared tooling found the same blind spot and widened the kit's copy of the gate. this archive does not use the kit's copy; it runs its own tools/check-living.py, so the fix did not reach it and had to be made here.

measured before it was changed: the leak was zero. a first crude search looked like three hits and every one was a published dead namesake — joachim luwinski born 1865, sally leibholz, gertrud leibke. the blind spot was real and the leak was not, which is the order those two things have to be established in.

and it was proved rather than assumed. a scratch copy of the build was given a served atlas-data.json naming a guarded living person, with nothing in the html. the old gate answered “ok” and exited zero. the new one named the file, the person and the matched text, and failed the build.
two rules for this particular family

on the holocaust records. dates and places come from the bundesarchiv and are quoted as the bundesarchiv gives them, including its refusals: where it declines to state a date of death because the date is not certain, this archive declines too, and says why. jacob leibholz has no death date here. that is not an omission.

on the paternity. it is stated, because burying a documented inconsistency in a private file would make the rest of the archive worth less. it is labelled as an inference, the arithmetic is shown, and the tests that would overturn it are listed. dna match holders are living people and are not named.
four ways an instrument lied, in one week

every one of these produced a confident, well-written, wrong answer, and every one of them survived review because it looked like careful work. they are set out because the rules they yield are worth more than the findings they nearly destroyed.
a common-name control cannot clear a rare-name negative 22 september 2026

twelve berlin telephone volumes were swept for the surname leipholz. the search found it in four and nothing in eight, and the eight were false. the ocr prints the name leiphotz, lelpholz, leipkslz and leibholz — five of the eleven readable volumes mangle it, and a search for the correct spelling misses every one.

what licensed the error was a control that looked healthy the whole time: schmidt, 133 to 191 hits a volume, in every book with a text layer. that proves the layer exists. it proves nothing about whether one broken glyph ate a rare string, and a volume can be richly indexed and still lose one line.

the instrument that works is the alphabet, because it does not depend on the glyph being right. the name falls in a known slot — leipholz sorts between leipert and leipic — so the whole slot is printed and read, and an absence is recorded only when a name above it and a name below it are both in hand. a missing side is inconclusive, not negative. eight unreliable zeros became six positives and two real absences, and two published claims turned out to be wrong.

a corollary found the same week, reading the adressbuch: the slot method reproduced two counts already read at the image (seventeen householders in 1938, ten in 1940) and then failed predictably where the ocr loses the typographic dashes. a method that states where it stops is worth more than one that quietly under-reports.
the landesarchiv’s own finder has a defect, and it is not consistent 22 september 2026
labsa, the berlin register finder, offers births, marriages and deaths as three checkboxes. ticking more than one does not widen the search — it corrupts it:
¦query volumes returned
¦standesamt schöneberg, deaths alone 61
¦standesamt schöneberg, all three ticked 0
¦standesamt charlottenburg, deaths alone 7
¦standesamt charlottenburg, all three ticked 8

not the sum of anything, and not even reliably zero. a count from the combined form is not a count and a zero from it is not an absence. this archive’s existing work was then checked against the defect rather than assumed safe: the sixty-one schöneberg death volumes it rests on are exactly the single-checkbox figure, so nothing published was disturbed.
guessing at names is not enumerating them 23 september 2026

the charlottenburg registry holdings were inventoried by querying the five office names the archive could think of: 143 volumes in five designations. the real figure is 207 in six. it had missed standesamt charlottenburg von berlin entirely, because labsa matches an office name exactly and the list of names is only obtainable from the form’s own autocomplete endpoint.

the same root produced a factual error on kurt’s page, which said jacob’s 1913 office was “one of charlottenburg i to iv”. charlottenburg iv did not exist in 1913 — its earliest volume of any kind is 1922. correction 9500913.
a tenth of a catalogue went missing, and the hole was shaped like an umlaut 23 september 2026

with the office names finally in hand, the whole free holding was enumerated: 5,383 name-index volumes across 139 offices — 2,845 death, 1,595 marriage, 943 birth. that single list turns several jobs this archive had been costing by eye into finite ones: reinickendorf’s remaining death indexes are thirteen volumes, and the whole of “she died in some other borough” is 296 volumes across 25 offices.

the first pass reported 4,838 volumes and said twenty-nine offices held nothing — and all twenty-nine have an umlaut or an eszett in the name. schöneberg, neukölln, köpenick, weißensee. the autocomplete hands names back double-encoded and the search needs them that way, but the results table prints them correctly encoded, so the loop queried in one form and filtered the returned rows on the other. every query succeeded; every row was then discarded. a quiet, confident zero, twenty-nine times, worth 545 volumes.

it was caught by a control and by nothing else. schöneberg has sixty-one death volumes — a figure this archive already rested on and had pulled by hand an hour earlier — and the new catalogue said zero. the fault was not in the archive’s instrument but in the code reading it, which is the harder kind to see: nothing errored, and 4,838 looked plausible.
what the slot method then bought 23 september 2026

applied to reinickendorf’s thirteen outstanding death-index volumes, read through pdf.js over http range requests — 807 pages of 2,120 out of some 700 mb, nothing downloaded — it closed a borough: with the run already read to 1981, twenty-one consecutive years of friedrich leipholz’s own borough, 1974 to 1994, and his death is not registered there.

and the first pass of that sweep was discarded. it had tested whether each volume’s alphabet was open on both sides of leibholz and then reported thirteen negatives covering leipholz too. those are two different slots. in the 1990 volume the nearest name above leibholz is leipe, which sorts below leipholz — so that slot had never been shown to be read at all. the claim would have been true and unearned. two volumes also failed mid-read with network errors and were not counted as absences: a failed fetch is not an absence.
the sweep’s one positive is on the leibholz page — marie leipholz, the only leipholz in all twenty-one years, dying in the borough friedrich lived in.
corrections to the source

where a named source overrides the family record, the correction is applied to the register and listed here with the evidence. nothing is silently rewritten — the original value is carried through as was, so a reader can always see what the family believed and why this archive disagrees.
23 corrections are listed, each with what the family record said, what this archive says instead and the evidence, on the corrections page.
duplicate records in the source

the tree holds five people twice. each pair shares an identical birth and death date, so these are not two people with one name — they are one person entered twice, usually once with parents attached and once without. they are collapsed here to the fuller copy, and listed so the collapse can be checked or reversed.
¦person dropped kept
¦gertrud leibke (leibholz) 9500145 9500104
¦georg leibholz 9500151 9500026
¦julius leibke 9500148 9500152
¦henriette katz (leibke) 9500149 9500153
¦leopold leibke 9500150 9500154

one of these mattered. the dateless copy of leopold leibke was the only record in the whole tree flagged as a living person without a birth year — while the fuller copy of the same man records his death in 1932. the build's living-persons check caught it, which is what the check is for.
and an exception, made deliberately 15 september 2026

two more people are now named who may be living: linda a wear, born 1933, and bruce w wear, born 1936 — two of the six children of henry robert wear and martha maud castle. they were withheld for a few hours this evening under the rule below, and then restored at the family's direction.

the reasoning is worth setting down, because the rule is otherwise absolute. the sibship is the argument: what identifies derrick's biological father is that the couple had exactly two sons and the younger was eleven years old in 1948. withholding the younger son's name while relying on his existence and his age is a strange kind of privacy — it publishes the fact that matters about him and hides only the label.

so they appear as the general register office index has them and in no other way: a name, a quarter, a district. no addresses, no descendants, no dates beyond the quarter of registration, and nothing inferred about either of them. neither is suggested to be anybody's father. if either of them, or anyone acting for them, would rather not be here, write and they come out the same day.
one living person is named with less than the others, and that is all that is published about him

4 other living people are named, with their relationships, town and country, and nothing more (living people, above). the last — lynn derrick luwinski — is named with less still, because the archive is about his ancestry and cannot be written without saying whose it is.

named is the whole of it. no birth date, and — since 14 september 2026 — no birth year either. a year is a date of birth with the precision filed off, and paired with a full name it is the half of an identity that is worth stealing. it was removed from the pages, from the generated register, and from the builder that writes the register, so that a rebuild cannot quietly restore it.

facts that gave the year away by arithmetic went with it: his age at his father's death, his age when the first divorce action was filed, the interval between the wedding and the birth. the events are still here — a child was born, and it was after the wedding — because they carry the argument. the dates attached to him are not, because they carried nothing but him.
a false claim of kinship, caught before it was sent corrected
a request for ivone's porto death record had been drafted months ago and never sent. read again before sending on 15 september 2026, it contained the line “sou neto dela” — i am her grandson.

it is not true. ivone's son is derrick. the researcher is the son of derrick's former wife by her second marriage, and is no relation to ivone at all — a fact his own dna test states plainly, his father being that second husband. the sentence would have put a false statement of relationship in front of a government registry.

it was also unnecessary. a portuguese certidão de óbito is a public document and needs no claim of kinship at all. the line now says only that the purpose is genealogical and non-commercial. check who you are claiming to be before you claim it — an archive that writes to registries under a borrowed relationship is worth nothing, however good its intentions.
spellings are evidence, not noise

on 20 september 2026 a shared tidying tool offered this archive two changes, and held them back because each alters a letter in a name: luwinsky → luwinski, across eighteen places, and hostowski → hostowsky. it was right to ask. both were refused.

every one of those eighteen luwinsky tokens is doing one of two jobs. some are quoting a document: the witwatersrand court index reads “kurt luwinsky versus ivone (born mota figueiredo)”, and that is the spelling the registrar typed. the rest are deliberate lists of the variants — the rule at the head of the lines page, the forms on the names page, and the record of what was searched in the bounded negatives. folding them would have turned “searched luwinski and luwinsky” into “searched luwinski and luwinski”, which is not a tidier sentence but a false account of work already done.

and the second fold runs the wrong way. kurt's second wife appears as hostovsky on the 1956 marriage register, hostowski in the cape town and wynberg register, and hostowsky in the 1957 divorce. the tool proposed collapsing them onto hostowsky. the form this archive has argued for as her birth name is hostovsky, on the most formal of the three documents — so the fold would have enshrined the wrong one and destroyed the other two. her three forms are now set out on the names page with the document each belongs to, which is what this archive does with a spelling instead of normalising it.

the underlying worry was fair: an archive that writes a name three ways looks careless. this one writes it three ways because three clerks did, and it now says so in the place a reader would look. the rule: quoted spellings are never altered, variant lists are never collapsed, and where the archive speaks in its own voice it says which form it has chosen and why.
and the tool was corrected, so this page should not be read as a standing complaint 21 september 2026

the refusals above stand — those two particular folds are still wrong for this archive's content. but the tool that proposed them has since changed, and the change answers the objection. where an archive spells a name several ways it now names the label it used and says it is only a label, and the map is applied to the search query and to the stored row alike, so every form finds every other and nothing claims any one of them is correct.

that matters for a distinction this archive leaned on hard on 20 september. a fold of this kind is a search rule with no concept of identity. it says these letters find those rows, not these people are those people — which is exactly the line between leipholz reaching willi and jenny, who are ours to consider, and leipholz reaching an eighteenth-century protestant family at orzysz-arys in masuria, who are certainly not. the variant list widens the search. it must never widen the family.
where the evidence for a bug lives
three instruments failed silently in one day, and none of the three failures was visible in the case in front of it.

the landesarchiv's registry database. four offices returned nothing and this archive nearly published “schöneberg has no online name index.” the database stores its office names double-encoded, so the correct spelling finds nothing and the mangled one finds seventeen volumes. the tell was that all four failures contained an umlaut and none of the successes did.

geneteka. both spellings of a surname returned an empty table, and both were nearly written down as zeroes. the province and record-type parameters had been left blank, and a blank parameter there is not “everywhere” but “nothing”. the control caught it.

a shared tidying tool, in a peer's archive: a change of selection rule quietly took a working map from 1,495 rows back to 59. it was caught by regenerating the map and reading it, not by reading the code.

in all three the evidence was in the set, not in any one case — a shared character across the failures, a shape of query that differed from the control, a count that moved. none of it is visible from inspecting a single result, and none of it was found by reasoning about how the tool ought to behave. hence the standing rule that a negative is only worth recording if a positive control went down the same path, and the addition earned today: when several negatives have something in common, suspect the thing they have in common before believing the negatives.
why this archive's menu differs from its siblings

seven related archives share a spine of the families and people & places. this one runs start · our line · places · people & names · evidence, and the difference has never been written down. a deviation nobody has recorded is indistinguishable from drift, so here is the reason.

“our line” rather than “the families” because the question this archive exists to answer is a single descent — whether derrick is kurt's son — and the pages under it are the people that question runs through. a families group would invite a second and a third family that are not the subject.

“people & names” rather than “people & places” because the naming is not incidental here, it is the obstacle. ivone is filed under six spellings of her maiden surname, three forenames and four married surnames. kurt's own name has eight recorded forms, and on 20 september an eighth — leipholz — turned out to be the one that reached people the other seven could not. places have their own group already.

the spine is a myheritage family tree of 164 people, read on 14 september 2026. it is a family record, not an archive: it carries real documents, real citations, family estimates and at least two duplicated individuals, all mixed together at the same apparent confidence. separating those is most of the work here. where this archive contradicts the tree — jacob's death year, georg's parentage, the february 1948 marriage — the contradiction is set out with its evidence rather than quietly corrected.

blocks: what has been read, and what has only been identified
named so that every claim on this site can be traced back, and so that the gap between what is actually held and what is merely known to exist stays visible.

of the 23 sources this archive has read, 23 now say where they are — the one that carries no link is a scan the family holds, and it says so. the six below it are named and not yet reached, which is what that heading means.
yad vashem, central database of shoah victims’ names
collections.yadvashem.org

searched properly on 17 september 2026, having previously been used for one list only. leibholz returns 88 victim records across the list of murdered jews from germany, the list of deportation from berlin, eighteen pages of testimony and the theresienstadt inmate list. jacob’s record (13520936) names the train: “transport 30 from berlin to auschwitz birkenau on 26/02/1943”, and gives his citizenship as german. oskar’s (13449776) gives theresienstadt 17 march 1943, auschwitz 16 october 1944, and death the same day. it also identifies a source this archive had been quoting at second hand without knowing it: the gedenkbuch berlins der jüdischen opfer des nationalsozialismus, freie universität berlin, edition hentrich, berlin 1995 — berlin’s own memorial book, not the national one, and the origin of the transport number.
collections.arolsen-archives.org

the international centre on nazi persecution, some 30 million documents referring to around 17.5 million people. index read 17 september 2026; the documents were not opened. 213 person entries under leibholz. it confirms, from a body of records entirely separate from the bundesarchiv, jakob leibholz 08.08.1884 schubin, oskar leibholz 13.05.1887 schubin and siegfried leibholz 05.08.1925; it carries two of the brothers under the compulsory name — leibholz, israel oskar and leibholz, georg israel; it holds a post-war tracing case for oskar, t/d 52.971, fourteen documents; and it holds kurt himself. the documents stop here on purpose: opening one requires ticking a declaration of consent about the use of sensitive personal data, which is a statement a named person makes about their own conduct, and this archive does not tick it on anybody's behalf. everything cited is from the index, which needs no consent.
the link reaches the index, which needs no consent. opening a document requires ticking a declaration about sensitive personal data, and this archive does not tick it on anybody's behalf.
the national archives, discovery
discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk

the catalogue of kew and of more than two thousand five hundred other british archives. free, no account, answers json. first used on 17 september 2026, after two hundred and nineteen commits that cited kew references without once opening the catalogue they belong to. every citation on this site verifies, and two verify more precisely than they were published: wo 392/15 is specifically “section 5: south africa (union defence forces)”, which is exactly the claim made here about leonard wear; wo 329/1120 adds the page range 312–622. it also gave wo 372/4/50790, the item reference for frederick james castle’s medal card, and dp/12/1/14 and dp/12/1/15, the baldock baptism registers at hertfordshire archives. luwinski returns zero across every archive it describes. wrapped in tools/tna.py, which has a --verify mode. on 17 september that mode was run over the whole site: forty-four distinct archival references, forty-two verified exactly, two resolved after one correction, and none wrong, missing or misattributed. the two were the same mistake twice and it is not really ours — rg 15/7079 and rg 14/7576 carry a leading zero, which is how findmypast prints a piece number and not how kew does. the catalogue also confirmed the content: rg 11/574 is 5k st james bermondsey, ho 107/1560 is bermondsey (street indexed), rg 14/10304 is colchester south-east, and the three bt 27 pieces are southampton feb–mar 1937, london apr–jun 1939 and london aug–oct 1939 — leonard’s sailing, his father’s and his mother’s, in the right ports in the right months.
zentral- und landesbibliothek berlin, berliner adressbücher

the berlin city directories, digitised annually from 1799 to 1970, six to seven thousand pages a volume, listing householders by name, trade and street. free, full-text, json. read from 17 september 2026; wrapped in tools/zlb.py. 1,047 page hits for leibholz and 23 for luwinski. the counts by year, with controls, are in data/berlin-adressbuch.tsv. the ocr is fraktur and the columns jam — counting is reliable, reading a named line needs the page image.
www.findmypast.co.uk

, full subscription, from 16 september 2026 — the 1851, 1871, 1881, 1891, 1901, 1911 and 1921 censuses of england and wales; the 1939 register; the gro birth, marriage and death indexes; bt 27 outbound passenger lists; soldiers died in the great war; the first world war campaign medal rolls and medal index cards; wo 363 and wo 364 service records; british armed forces and overseas births, marriages and deaths; and hertfordshire baptisms. most of the wear and castle work on this site is from it. its transcripts are not the records: the 1911 barracks return that names frederick castle’s regiment has an empty occupation column in the transcript and reads scottish rifles on the image. worked through the australian site — www.findmypast.com.au and search.findmypast.com.au — which is where david’s subscription lives and what every link in this archive’s data points at, though the records are the same british ones.
familysearch full-text search
www.familysearch.org/search/full-text

, signed in, 17 september 2026 — which reads the words on unindexed images rather than a name index. luwinski, luwinsky, luwenski and the phrase piccadilly hat: thirty-three hits and every one american. the control ran first and the corpus really does hold south africa — but what it holds is the voters’ rolls of 1925–1931, and every person this archive wants arrived after the last roll was printed.

a free mirror of the south african archives index with death and estate databases attached, and it does stem matching where the official index does not. it answered in four seconds a question that had taken a day, and produced three luwinski court files nobody had seen.

geneteka, the polish genealogical society’s volunteer index
geneteka.genealodzy.pl

put to this family three times and useful every time for the same reason — it says what it does not hold. warmińsko-mazurskie: its 278 parishes include olsztyn and reszel and their civil registries and do not include bössau, biesowo, jeziorany or zerbuń, which are the two places kurt’s mother’s family actually came from. pomorskie, 11 october 2026: of the eleven west prussian and pomeranian towns the gedenkbuch’s fifty leibholz cluster in, nine are not indexed at all — człuchów (schlochau) and czarne (hammerstein) among them — and of the two that are, przechlewo stops before 1800 and debrzno, which is preussisch friedland, stops before 1840. and the province holds essentially no jewish records: births give schmidt 1,134 and kowalski 1,023 against cohn 1, levy 0, levin 0 and israel 1, so a jewish surname’s zero in this index is the index speaking and is never recorded here as a negative. two warnings for anyone using it: the province codes are positional and an invalid one falls back silently to dolnośląskie, which cost this archive a day in september; and the results are an ajax call, so the html page returns an empty table and the rows come from api/getact.php.
landesarchiv berlin — labsa, the namensverzeichnisse to berlin’s civil registers
content.landesarchiv-berlin.de/labsa/show/index.php

the public viewer of the name indexes to berlin’s birth, marriage and death registers — free, no account, no fee — and the instrument behind every berlin register reading on this site. worked from 7 october 2026; wrapped in tools/labsa.py. over 600 volumes have been passed through it and roughly 150 read entire, across neukölln, kreuzberg, reinickendorf, spandau, schöneberg and all eleven east berlin offices. three limits worth knowing before anyone uses it again. the record-type checkboxes do not union — ask for one kind per request or the answer is silently wrong. it cannot display umlauts: search an office on its stem (‘neuk’) and pick the mangled entry out of the list. and there are 150-odd registry offices with no index across them, each indexing births, marriages and deaths separately for every year, so an enquiry that cannot name the responsible standesamt cannot be answered at all. the label “durchsuchbares pdf durch ocr-texterkennung” is not a promise about the names. every volume on this site is scored against six common surnames before its silence is allowed to count, and the blind ones are recorded as unread rather than as negatives.

on the family tree as a source

it is a good tree and it is not an archive. it carries certified citations alongside family estimates, at the same apparent weight, and it contains at least two duplicated people. three of its statements are contradicted here on the evidence: jacob leibholz's death year, georg leibholz's parentage, and the february 1948 marriage date. that is not a complaint. a tree that records what the family believed is exactly the right thing to start from, and the corrections were only possible because it recorded enough to be checked.

the fault this page was built to close 17 september 2026

this archive kept twenty-one evidence files in data/ — censuses, the gedenkbuch, the 1939 register, passenger lists, court files. not one build script read any of them. the register was assembled from the myheritage export and corrections.json and nothing else. everything a record actually said reached this site only because a human retyped it into a paragraph.

that is survivable while the human is paying attention and silently wrong the moment they are not. nothing would have noticed if a file had been added and never surfaced, or if a page and a file had come to disagree. there was no gate, because there was nothing to gate.

the clearest casualty was samuel israel leibholz. the register printed his birth as “june 28 1877?” — with the source tree’s question mark intact — while data/leibholz-gedenkbuch.tsv held the bundesarchiv’s entry en909753, giving 28 june 1877 at schubin, and his death at auschwitz on 10 april 1943. the archive had the citation. the page showed the doubt.
what this page does not do

it does not rewrite the tree. the register and the charts draw the export as given, and that rule has not changed: the question mark on samuel’s birth year is still there, because that is what the source says. what has changed is that the record sits beside it instead of in a file nobody reads. where a named source genuinely overrides the family record that is a correction, shown as was and now, and it is a different mechanism on purpose.

absences, with the limits that make them worth something.
why this page exists

several of this archive’s conclusions now rest on absences. that leonard has no south african estate. that ivone never naturalised. that the marriage registers never asked for parents. each of those is only worth something because somebody measured how far the search reached — and until now those measurements lived in commit messages and working notes, where a later reader would never find them.
the distinction the page is trying to hold is between this is not there and i did not find it. the first is a finding. the second is a shrug. the column that separates them is the last one.
kurt luwinski's estate was never advertised in the south african government gazette — or the scanner lost it

searched: gazettes.africa, the full south african run. luwinski and luwinsky, every year; then the ocr manglings luwinsk, luwenski, lnwinski, luwiuski, luwinshi; then lewinski, whose two hits in 1969 and 1970 were opened.

result: eight documents in the entire corpus, and not one is his estate: three in october 1942 (16th, 23rd, 30th) dissolving the partnership between walter oppenheimer and kurt luwinski, three in november 1941 (7th, 14th, 21st) creating it, one in november 1972 for paula luwinski and one in july 1975 for paula luwinski at pallou's dress centre, 18 wanderers street. that enumeration was wrong here until 22 september 2026 and the error was this page's alone: it said eight and then listed six, giving two november 1941 notices instead of three and omitting the 1975 one altogether. the kurt page has carried all eight correctly throughout, and so has the work list. re-counted against the live search, which still returns exactly eight. nothing at all in 1968, 1969, 1970 or 1971. the two lewinski hits are both von lewinsky in a tariff list.

what would fall outside it: the control is what makes this worth anything, and it kills the innocent explanation. the years are fully in the corpus and full of exactly the kind of notice that is missing: searching 1969 for 'estates of deceased persons' returns 221 issues, 'boedel' returns 100, 'master of the supreme court' returns 111; 1970 gives 163, 93 and 101. so this is not a gap in the archive of gazettes. what it still cannot distinguish: a notice the scanner mis-read from a notice that was never placed. the search does no prefix matching — 'luwinsk' returns zero where 'luwinski' returns eight — so a mangled spelling is invisible to it, and this corpus has already been caught rendering figueiredo as 'epo .figueiredo,carlosde'. he died on 15 december 1968 and his estate is mhg 7584/69. only the file itself can say which.
leonard aubrey robert wear is in no south african record familysearch holds except his two marriages

searched: all thirty-two south african collections familysearch holds, found by enumerating all 3,502 of its collections and filtering. surname wear matched exactly - 111 records, every one read - then repeated under ware, weir, wier, weare, wearne and wears.

result: he appears twice. johannesburg, 7 september 1940, to phyllis agnes robertson, aged 23. johannesburg, 30 october 1951, to marjorie eileen dunlop, aged 34. no death, no burial, no estate, no baptism, under any spelling.

what would fall outside it: and here is why it proves less than it looks, which is the point of writing it down. familysearch's south african civil death registration is a name index to 1966: exact-year counts give 61,899 for 1960, 74,131 for 1965, 59,263 for 1966 - and then 178 for 1967 and nothing after it. leonard died in 1973 or 1979. his absence from an index that ends seven years before he died is not evidence about him. the same bound removes kurt, who died in 1968, and henry robert, who died in september 1969 and is nonetheless in the collection - as a burial, in the johannesburg cemetery registers, which run to 2019. so the negative that does carry weight is the narrower one: he was not buried in a johannesburg cemetery, in a set that holds his father, his mother and two later wears.
there is no post-1970 south african marriage register to reach by name on familysearch
searched: "south africa, civil marriage records, 1801-1974", collection 2821281 - 2,556,837 records and 2,692,991 images. counted by exact year rather than trusting the title.

what would fall outside it: a cliff, not a decline. the collection is titled 1801-1974 and is, as a name index, 1801-1960. the images may well run to 1974; nothing lets you find one by name. the general lesson, and this archive has now learned it twice in a week: a collection's title describes the records, not the index, and an index that stops looks exactly like a family that leaves no record. the first time was the electoral registers, where a search box returned 3,478 rows and not one name.
leonard did not die in england or wales between 1970 and 1985 16 sep 2026

searched: freebmd (the gro death index for england and wales): surname wear, deaths, march 1970 to december 1985, no forename given — 241 entries across 58 consecutive quarters widened 22 september 2026 with freebmd's own phonetic flag. the original searched wear as an exact string. soundex wear, deaths, mar 1970 to dec 1985 returns 6,664 matches — twenty-seven times the exact-spelling pool, and the first search never saw any of it. narrowed by the forename leonard it comes to about forty entries across weir, ware, warr, wray, whear, wyer, were, wroe, werry, whurr, wier and werra.

result: sixteen of the 241 were born between 1915 and 1919. not one is leonard aubrey robert wear; the only 1917 birth is a sam wear of halifax. a separate search on the forename leonard returns one man, leonard rigby wear, born 10 october 1897, died claro june 1970. and the widened search does not disturb it. of the forty phonetic leonards, exactly one is a true wear — leonard rigby wear, born 10 october 1897, died claro, june 1970 — and not one of the forty was born in 1917. leonard aubrey robert wear was born at hitchin in the first quarter of 1917. freebmd prints a date of birth against every death registered after 1969, which is what makes this decisive rather than suggestive: it is not that no matching name was found, it is that every candidate name was found and every one of them is a different man with a different birth year.

what would fall outside it: as clean as a negative gets, and the reasons are worth stating. every one of the 58 quarters is marked >99% complete, and freebmd's own coverage chart shows 1970–1983 at 100%. from 1969 the gro death index carries full forenames and the date of birth, so he could hide behind neither an initial nor a common surname. what it does not cover: deaths abroad, which are in the consular and overseas registers and have not been searched; and scotland and northern ireland, which have separate registers. what the widening does not fix. freebmd is not complete. its own coverage pages say so, and a death it has not yet transcribed is invisible to any spelling. the negative is about the gro index as freebmd has it, not about the gro index.
the british consular and overseas registers cannot contain leonard's death 16 sep 2026
searched: gro consular death series coverage; gov.uk guidance on registering a death abroad; published lists of excluded countries

result: three separate exclusions, all pointing the same way. the consular death registers run 1849–1965, so both candidate years fall outside. the modern statutory service covers deaths “on or after 1 january 1983” and is optional. and south africa appears on the published list of countries where a death cannot be registered with the british authorities at all.

what would fall outside it: the first two are firm — a series end-date and gov.uk's own words. the third is probable, not proven: it is a local authority's summary, not legislation, and is marked as such. any one of the three would be enough on its own.
leonard has no deceased estate in south africa 15 sep 2026
searched: national archives (naairs), all repositories, surname wear, 1970–1976
result: no wear deceased estate in the transvaal at all between 1970 and 1976. the last is his father's, mhg 10245/69.

what would fall outside it: the estate index stops at the end of 1976 — 2,246 estate records in 1976, one in 1977, zero after. so 1973 is inside the index and he is not in it; 1979 is three years past its last year and cannot be tested this way at all. || and a bound added 27 september 2026 that is not about the index but about the database. every bound this archive wrote for its naairs nils concerns the index's coverage of the records — which series are indexed at item level, where the estate index stops. none concerns the database's coverage of the index, because on 15-16 september there was no reason to think there were two databases. there are. narssa's own search page states it, verified at source 27 september: "narssa is in the process of migrating more than 8.3 million entries from the old naairs database to the new database and therefore 'fulltext search' (new database) will not display all the records in the system. in the meantime narssa makes both databases available for use by the public. using the 'search old naairs database' will provide a more complete search." what this archive can show about which one answered, and it is evidence not proof: the vocabulary of these searches is the old database's — "all repositories", "national registers", "central-government database", the repository code rsae — and the new fulltext search has no such repository selection. the 16 september searches name the endpoint www.national.archsrch.gov.za/sm300cv/smws/sm300dl, which is the classic search manager service, i.e. the old complete one. probed again 27 september: it answers 503, and the old portal page naairs.htm is now 404. so the balance of evidence is that the old complete database answered. it is not established for the 15 september searches, whose pre-move entry point was never written down as a url. the nil stands and is now bounded: it was taken from a service that had a partial twin, and this archive did not check which twin it was talking to. raised by a peer session, verified here at narssa's own page.
leonard is not buried in any johannesburg cemetery the index covers 15 sep 2026
searched: familysearch personas, f.collectionid=4453927 (johannesburg cemetery registers, 1840–2019), surname wear, all 517 hits

result: six distinct wears: henrietta 1909, henry robert 1969, martha maud 1986, edwina ann 2014, michelle ann 2017, dan b undated. no leonard, under any spelling of his forenames. he bought grave 56045 and was not buried in it.

what would fall outside it: this is the indexed layer of one collection. it does not cover unindexed images within it, other johannesburg cemeteries, or the chevrah kadisha — a separate database, and the one holding kurt, pauline and salkow. a wear would have no business in a jewish cemetery, but the exclusion is stated rather than assumed.
leonard aubrey robert wear was granted no probate in england and wales between 1970 and 1981 — and it took three wrong answers before this archive actually read the calendar 15 sep 2026

searched: probatesearch.service.gov.uk (find a will). originally: surname wear, year of death 1973, keyword aubrey. re-examined 22 september 2026, three times, because the first two re-examinations were both wrong. what finally settled it was reading the request instead of the page. the service answers in two halves. the digital half holds only grants issued from 1996 and says so, so a 1973 query returns 0 before anything is searched. the image half calls an ocr full-text endpoint, pp_cowindex_default_search, over the scanned calendar broken into chunks named for the first surname on them. called directly, that endpoint plainly works: wear 1973 returns 41 chunks, smith 1973 returns 469, and luwinski and the nonsense string zqxvwyrk return 0. two of the 41 bracket the name alphabetically — 009223_weake_1973.pdf (weake to weare) and 009225_wearmouth_1973.pdf (wearmouth to weatherby). and then, the same evening, the calendar was actually read. the chunk's ocr text is served as a property, textract:doccontent, so the page never has to be rendered. four chunks were read in full: 009223_weake_1973.pdf (weake to weare, so the whole of wear), 009474_wear_1974.pdf, 008820_weale_1979.pdf and 009151_wear_1980.pdf. the two following years were read because the calendar is ordered by year of grant, not year of death — the 1973 volume contains people who died in december 1972. separately the forename pair “leonard aubrey” was put to every year from 1970 to 1981. controls first this time: “ernest leslie” in 1973 returns 18, the nonsense string returns 0, and wear/smith/luwinski return 41/469/0 — the count moves with the name.

result: sixteen wear grants across the four years, read name by name, and not one is him. 1973: alfred, dorothy winifred, ellen, elsie, ernest leslie, james watson, mary rosine, william. 1974: walter. 1979: james william, arthur, charles, edith maud. 1980: annie ellen, norman, rosetta emma. and the wider test is the stronger one: “leonard aubrey” across 1970-1981 returns twenty-six men — bricknell, dinsmore, williams, day, hill, beniston, moore, barton, peters, waghorne, evans, hogben, pridole, webberley, howard, briers four times, cooper, hillier, palmer, hawkins, wines, bright, stuckey. not one is a wear.

what would fall outside it: what it does not settle: an english grant needs english assets, so a man who died in south africa need never appear in this calendar at all. this is a negative about a route, not about a life. and it rests on ocr — the very page that was read prints “milliam” for william and “minifred” for winifred — which is why the surname blocks were counted off the page rather than returned by a query. and the road here is kept because it is the useful part. this archive published three wrong answers about this one negative in a single evening: a zero read from the half of the service that structurally cannot hold a 1973 grant; then a control that had not been repeated; then a printed count — “41 document pages returned” — that turns out to be a defect in the service's own page, identical for every surname, for nonsense, and for both years. the fault behind all three was reading the rendered page instead of the request underneath it. what finally worked was calling the endpoint, running a positive and a null control before believing anything, and then reading the actual words on the actual page.
ivone never naturalised as a south african 15 sep 2026

frederick james castle has no surviving first world war service file — and that is what a career soldier looks like, not a gap

searched: findmypast, british army service records — which carries wo 363, the 'burnt documents', and wo 364, the pension claims — surname castle, forename fred*, all 78 results read across four pages, 17 september 2026.

result: not one entry for the scottish rifles, the cameronians, or service number 10061. there are fred james castles in the set — 98411 labour corps, 10524 devonshire regiment, 40524 13th reserve cavalry — and every one of them belongs to another man; the labour corps one is the royal berkshire soldier whose medal card gives 33601 and 98411 together.
frederick james castle did not die on army service abroad and did not marry in an army chapel abroad — under that name

searched: findmypast, 17 september 2026. british armed forces and overseas deaths and burials: surname castle, forename fred*, all ten results accounted for. british armed forces and overseas banns and marriages: surname castle, all fifty-nine results read across three pages. these are the registers a soldier of the 1920s appears in instead of the ordinary general register office series.

result: nothing in either. no scottish rifles death and no number 10061; the nearest by name is frederick j castle who died in 1917 and is private 47783 of the northumberland fusiliers, buried at roclincourt valley cemetery in france. in the marriage set there is not one fred, frederick or fredk among fifty-nine castles, who marry instead at malta, kolar, istanbul, singapore, italy, aldershot and johannesburg.
the name luwinski appears in no record described by any archive in the national archives' discovery catalogue

searched: discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk, the catalogue of the national archives and of more than two thousand five hundred other british archives — county record offices, university and cathedral libraries, regimental and company collections. searched 17 september 2026 for luwinski and luwinsky, and re-run 21 september 2026 across fourteen spellings: luwinski, luwinsky, luwenski, luwinsk, lowinski, lewinski, and the eight leibholz forms leibholz, leipholz, leybholz, laibholz, leibholtz, leipholtz, leibolz, leiphols.

result: count 0 for both. by contrast leibholz returns sixteen, none of them ours — gerhard leibholz, dietrich bonhoeffer's brother-in-law, at lambeth palace library; a 1948 naturalisation certificate; two home office alien files; and an internment card for a tobias leibholz born at breslau in 1906. re-run 21 september under the eighth spelling and the negative holds and is now wider. luwenski and luwinsk also return count 0, so four spellings of the name are now bracketed rather than two. leipholz returns 0, as do leybholz, laibholz, leibholtz, leipholtz, leibolz and leiphols — so the sixteen leibholz records are the whole of what discovery holds under any spelling of that name. two neighbouring surnames do return, and are named here so nobody has to find them twice: lowinski returns 20 (thomas esmond lowinsky, the painter, 1892-1947) and lewinski returns 228. neither is this family and neither is claimed as one.
the bundesarchiv gedenkbuch holds no leibholz under any misspelling this archive had not already tried — and that turned out to be false

searched: apps.bundesarchiv.de/gedenkbuch, the free name box, ten spellings put to it on 22 september 2026: leibholz, laibholz, leibholtz, leipholz, leibolz, lebholz, leiholz, leibhold, leibholcz, lelbholz. the control term leibholz was re-run between the others four times and returned 50 every time, so every negative below sits between two proofs that the instrument was answering.

result: seven of the ten are clean zeros — leibholtz, leipholz, leibolz, lebholz, leiholz, leibholcz and lelbholz. leibhold returns one and it is a false positive: the entry is “passau, leibhold”, where leibhold is the man's forename and passau his surname. and laibholz returns two people this archive had never seen — georg laibholz born 1 january 1883 and lidia laibholz born 1884, both of berlin, both dead at auschwitz, and neither a duplicate of the georg and the lydia already among the fifty, who carry different birth dates and died at kulmhof. one vowel had been hiding two murdered people from every search run here.

what would fall outside it: what the zeros are worth is set by the control, and the control is strong: the same box returned 50 for leibholz immediately before and after the run. what they are not is a statement about the gedenkbuch's coverage — the memorial book is the murdered as the bundesarchiv has been able to reconstruct them, and a name absent from it may simply never have been reconstructed. and the run caught a fault in its own instrument: pressing return in that box does not submit the form. the first attempt entered five terms with the return key and read back “50 results” for every one — the previous page each time, because nothing had been sent. five negatives that were never tested would have entered this archive as five findings. they were caught because 50 is not a believable answer for five different misspellings, and the run was done again with a click on the button, giving 0, 50, 0, 1 and 0. the lesson is not about this form: a reading that does not change is not a reading, and a sweep that cannot tell a fresh answer from a stale page is measuring nothing.
sally leibholz's death cannot be found by searching the kuyavia-pomerania portal — the name is not indexed and the szubin deaths have no alphabetical index

searched: www.genealogiawarchiwach.pl, 22 september 2026. three searches with their controls. (1) town szubin, category akta zgonów — the death registers. (2) the same, category skorowidze zgonów — the alphabetical death indexes. (3) free text on the surname leibholz against the surname schmul as a control, schmul being the bride's family from the same town and the same decades.

result: (1) 190 death units across 20 teams — szubin has three registry offices, miasto and wieś i and wieś ii, and all are digitised. (2) zero skorowidze zgonów. birth and marriage skorowidze exist for szubin; death ones do not. (3) leibholz returns exactly one scan in a 228,278-person index — the 1874 marriage — while schmul returns 119 scans from 34 teams across 104 units.

what would fall outside it: the controls are what make this worth anything, and they were run first this time. the skorowidze zero is not a broken filter: the identical facet with akta zgonów returns 190. the single leibholz is not a dead search box: the same box returns 119 for the bride's surname. so the portal's index is rich for schmul and blind to leibholz, and a leibholz death at szubin — if one exists — would have to be read off the page rather than found. what this is not is evidence that he did not die at szubin. nothing here has been read; 190 units stand unopened, and with no death year to aim at, a man born in 1847 could be in any of them. and the stronger point is that szubin may be the wrong town altogether: this family moved again. kurt was born in berlin in 1912, the household is at chodowieckistraße in 1913, and jacob married in berlin in 1924. if sally went with his sons, he died in berlin, and the instrument for that is the landesarchiv berlin name indexes this archive already reads fluently. paging 190 szubin units before testing berlin is the expensive way round.
friedrich leipholz's death is not registered in reinickendorf — his own borough — in any year from 1974 to 1994

searched: landesarchiv berlin, p rep. 130, namensverzeichnisse zum sterberegister, standesamt reinickendorf. the 1974-1981 volumes were read on 21 september 2026 and the thirteen remaining, 1982 to 1994 (nr. 1478-1490), on 23 september, through pdf.js over http range requests — 807 pages of 2,120, out of roughly 700 mb, with nothing downloaded. not a name search: the ocr mangles this surname in five of eleven volumes elsewhere, so the test is to print the whole alphabetical slot and read it, recording an absence only when a name above it and a name below it are both in hand. both spellings were bracketed separately — leibholz falls between leh- and leic-, leipholz between lein- and leis-, and they are two different slots. the text layer was tested before the sweep rather than after: this series prints names ("blank franz erich 11.07. 1652"), unlike the kreuzberg volumes of the same period, and a frequency control on the first nineteen pages returned becker 6, berger 5, brandt 8 and schmidt 0 — right for pages that have not yet left the letter b.

result: twenty-one consecutive years read, all bracketed on both sides of both spellings, and he is in none of them. he is in the berlin telephone book at schwabstraße 4 in reinickendorf to 1973-74 and absent from the 1974-75 volume, so he leaves the record during 1974 and his own borough never registers his death. the first pass of this sweep was discarded: it bracketed only the leibholz slot and would have published thirteen negatives covering leipholz too — in the 1990 volume the nearest name above leibholz is leipe, which sorts below leipholz, so that slot had never been shown to be read. two volumes, 1992 and 1993, failed mid-read with network errors and were not counted as absences; both read clean on retry. the sweep's one positive: marie leipholz, sterberegister 1988 nr. 2306, the only leipholz in all twenty-one years, dying in the borough he lived in.

what would fall outside it: a death outside reinickendorf. he may have moved: the landesarchiv's full catalogue puts the whole of "some other berlin borough" at 296 death-index volumes across 25 offices — bounded, and no longer a vague elsewhere. or he may have died after 1994, which would make him about ninety-nine and puts him past the thirty-year closure. or he may simply have given up the telephone and lived on, which at eighty is not unusual: heinrich leibholz vanished from the berlin directory after 1942 and did not die until 1948. leaving a telephone book is not dying, and nothing here says he died in 1974 — only that he stopped being listed.
the rule this page is trying to enforce

do not publish a null you did not bound. twice this evening a search returned nothing and the nothing was the archive’s own fault: once because a page’s results were still loading, and once because a form field was posted empty. both looked exactly like an empty holding. neither was.
so a negative enters this archive with three things attached or it does not enter at all: what was searched, over what range, and what would still fall outside it.

/open-questions/.title: Open questions — The Luwinski Archive
blocks: ten things this archive cannot answer yet, in the order they are worth attacking
an archive is worth what its unanswered questions are worth. these are written so that anyone — a cousin, a stranger, an archivist — can pick one up and work it without asking permission.
1 what were ivone's parents' given names?

their surnames are known — the 1948 divorce file has her born mota figueiredo — but the given names are still blank, and every paper route has been blocked. a surname sweep on 14 september 2026 seemed to open a new front door — 27 figueiredo matches, 13 mota — and it was withdrawn the same evening: the figueiredo tag pairs her with a woman born before 1713, and myheritage states that the mota matches share no ancestral surname with derrick at all.
what would settle it

her porto death record, which names both parents outright, and the 1924 lourenço marques registration. on the dna side the useful matches remain the two already worked — 108.7 cm at second cousin's son, and 133.2 cm — whose families carry the surnames jorge, silvestre, conde, gaspar and matos.
2 who was derrick's biological father?

answered so far as records can: leonard aubrey robert wear, born hitchin, hertfordshire, 1917. the dna excludes kurt israel luwinski twice over - 0.0% ashkenazi where a quarter is required, and a y-dna haplogroup, r-s11477 of r1b branch u106/z381, that is north sea rather than ashkenazi. the chain to a name: the 1952 johannesburg register gives the birthplaces of the closest match's grandparents, mervin halsey cape province and cynthia wear england, so the english link is the grandmother; cynthia's gro birth entry (q2 1931, hitchin, 3a/1345) gives her mother's maiden name as castle; the only wear-castle marriage in the whole english index is henry r wear to martha l castle, hitchin q4 1914; and the 1921 census has them at 72 pix road, letchworth. the shared segments then decided it. of the 297.5 cm derrick shares with that match, only about 44 fall in regions he also shares with any castle cousin - a single block on chromosome 2. the other 253 cm lie nowhere near them. two people who share only one ancestral couple cannot do that: he and she descend from henry robert wear and martha maud castle together, as a couple, so his father was their son. the birth index, searched on the mother's maiden name, gives that couple six children at hitchin between 1917 and 1936, of whom two were sons. in june 1948 one was thirty-one and the other was eleven. and the family emigrated entire: henry robert wear died in johannesburg on 11 september 1969 and is buried at west park, martha maud there on 16 march 1986. leonard was in johannesburg from 1940, married phyllis agnes robertson at rosebank on 7 september 1940, was divorced by her in 1951 and married again that october. corroborated from outside the dna: a seven-person myheritage tree kept by leonard's own daughter gives his mother as “muad wear, born castle”. no other record anywhere gives him parents at all.

the couple is proven to this archive's dna standard. that the son is leonard rests on the sibship - two sons, one of them a schoolboy - and not yet on a document naming him as anybody's father. request 11, drafted 15 september: the master of the high court at cape town, estates 10761/2024 (gillian agnes louisa nel, born wear, 1941-2024) and 018561/2021 (patricia mary maud grant, born wear, 1946-2021), both found free in the government gazette. each file holds a death notice, form j294, with a field for the father's full names. if either says leonard aubrey robert wear, a user-submitted tree becomes a government record. also outstanding: wld 1950/1948, the divorce kurt filed against ivone within months of marrying her, with wld 497/1951 and 2368/1951 behind it; mhg 10245/69, henry robert wear's own estate, whose death notice names his children; and leonard's own estate, once it is settled whether he died in 1973 or 1979. the y cannot help yet: only 34 of the 7,748 public members of the r-u106 project sit under s11477, whose common ancestor lived about 200 bce, and no wear, weir or ware is among them. a living male-line wear taking a y test would end it. gillian died in march 2024, so the half-sibling test that would have settled this in a single reading is gone.
3 why did auguste divorce jacob? (the when is answered: 21 march 1940)

half answered, 29 september 2026, and by the instrument this row named. the date is 21 march 1940 — landgericht berlin 251. r. 80. 40, rechtskräftig that day, noted in the margin of the couple's own marriage entry on 4 april 1940 and scanned by the landesarchiv berlin. this row said the answer would be in “the 5 january 1924 marriage entry that preceded them”, and it was. what is still open is the why, and a date is not a motive. in a berlin mischehe the pressure on the non-jewish wife to divorce was official and sustained, and divorce stripped the husband of his remaining protection — jacob was deported two years and eleven months later. nothing in the register says who petitioned or on what ground, and this archive will not guess at a motive it cannot see.

the landgericht berlin divorce case 251. r. 80. 40, if it survives in a court series. it is not in the marriage register's sammelakte — the landesarchiv has confirmed that file holds only the 1923 banns papers, so nobody should order it hoping for divorce material.
4 why did a german consulate treat kurt as a jew rather than a mischling? (where “israel” came from is answered)

answered 1 october 2026, from his own passport. this row used to reason that he left germany in 1933, six years before the compulsory-name decree, and that as a mischling he would have been outside it anyway — so the name looked like a family-tree embellishment. it is not. the german consulate in johannesburg issued him a passport on 26 july 1939 and he signed it “israel kurt luwinski” in his own hand. the decree of 17 august 1938 reached him six thousand miles from berlin, and he complied. what is still open is why: the document records the classification and gives no reason for it. the question is now about an act by a named office on a known day rather than about a word on a tree. and the row's own premise is separately in doubt: his berlin driving licence is dated 30 january 1934, so “he left in 1933” is itself no longer safe.

the consular file behind the 1939 passport, if it survives — deutsches konsulat johannesburg, july 1939 — which would say on what basis he was classified. failing that, a reichsvereinigung or jewish-community registration for the family in berlin.
5 is georg a brother or a cousin?
born at hammerstein two months after jacob was born at schubin. both dates from the bundesarchiv. they cannot both be sons of one mother.

asked, 15 september 2026. both towns are now in poland and both civil registries opened in 1874, so an 1884 birth entry names both parents outright. written to archiwum państwowe w bydgoszczy for standesamt schubin, and to archiwum państwowe w koszalinie for standesamt hammerstein and any jewish register covering sally leibholz, born there in 1847. if both entries survive, one line of each decides it.
the leibholz brothers
6 what happened to gertrud leibke on 27 february 1943?
she died in berlin, not in a camp, on the day of the fabrikaktion. the tree also duplicates her across two brothers.
berlin death register; merge the duplicate and establish which brother she married.
7 when did ivone actually marry de witt?
recorded as 2 february 1948, four and a half months before she married kurt, with no divorce between.
the germiston marriage register.
8 who was the pinto da rocha?

henrique's father, and the tree can only call him "unknown da rocha". located, 14 september 2026: henrique's south african deceased estate, gazetted three times in 2023 — estate 12294/2023, da rocha, henrique figueiredo pinto. a south african estate file contains the death notice, form j294, and that form asks for the full names of the father and the maiden name of the mother.

order the j294 from the master of the high court quoting 12294/2023. then his 1968 marriage record, which unlike the 1948 form does carry parents. and in parallel a letter to the arquivo da defesa nacional: he turned twenty five weeks after the colonial war began, and a portuguese military registration names both parents.
9 does jacob have a stolperstein?
none found in schöneberg. the leibholz stones located so far belong to other leibholz families.
koordinierungsstelle stolpersteine berlin. if there is none, there could be.
10 do any of the 100 index luwinskis connect?
not one has been shown to. they may be entirely unrelated people who share a rare surname.
allenstein and kreis rössel catholic registers, for joachim born 1865 and back.
nothing at that state.
written out in full in requests/ — the porto one in portuguese and english, ready to send.
conservatória do registo civil do porto — death and burial of ivone de figueiredo, b. 4 march 1922 lourenço marques.
arquivo histórico de moçambique, maputo, and the arquivo histórico ultramarino, lisbon — lourenço marques civil registration, 1924 and c. 1941.
landesarchiv berlin — schöneberg marriage 5 january 1924; the divorce file; kurt's 1912 birth entry; gertrud leibke's death, 27 february 1943.
arolsen archives — jacob, samuel, georg, oskar, elli and werner leibholz.
master of the supreme court, pretoria — estate file 7584/1969, kurt luwinski.
national archives of south africa — the 1948 and 1951 divorce actions, and the germiston marriage register.

/errands/.title: Errands — The Luwinski Archive
blocks: 10 drafted and not yet sent · 18 sent — 4 answered, 3 acknowledged but not yet answered, 11 silent, and 14 due to be chased
only this archive's letters. the same mailbox carries correspondence for the sibling archives, which is tracked there.
why this page exists

this archive has eighteen letters out for its own research alone — more again in the sibling archives that share the mailbox — and had no schedule for chasing any of them, which means they get chased either too early, which annoys archivists, or never, which is worse. it had already sent one correspondent two emails in four hours and a second correspondent a duplicate enquiry it had forgotten making.

so each letter now carries an interval chosen for the recipient, not a single global one. a parish office open three hours a day is not a commercial researcher. a national archive in another hemisphere is not a man who has quoted for work. the page recomputes on every build, so the dates below are live rather than written down once and forgotten.
drafted, and not yet sent

ten letters are written and waiting on david. they are kept here rather than in the work list, because a letter that exists and has not gone out is an errand and not a research question. this archive drafts; it does not send. each one is a file under requests/ in the repository. they are listed in the order to send them. a person who is waiting on an answer comes first, then a correction to something already sent, then the requests that could open the most of the kurt and ivone gaps, and the ones that touch other families come last. five drafts that stood here as unsent had gone out on 15 to 17 september; they are counted with the sent letters below and kept in requests/ as records.
¦order to what it asks why here, and before sending

¦1 landesarchiv berlin — ms oberle, answering her reply of 29 september39-reply-to-landesarchiv-oberle.txt thanks her, and supplies the one fact she said was missing: the standesamt for kurt luwinski's 1912 birth, berlin viii, entry 963, with the reasoning so that she can check it. adds gertrud leibholz's maiden name for her register, confirms what the divorce note settles, and asks one question before a paid order of the 1923 banns papers: whether they usually include both parties' birth certificates. places no order. german. first. reply on her thread of 29 september (a new thread, not the one of 14 september). a named archivist has been waiting since the 29th for the one fact she asked for, and it opens the route to kurt's birth entry. the birth entry itself is then ordered through the digitaler antrag (work list row 226), which costs money and is david's. delete the older draft of 20 september in the mailbox.

¦10 national archives of australia31-send-this-to-naa.txt an access examination request covering five luwinski and leibholz items, 1939 to 1965. four of the five are already open and are listed so the reference staff can answer for the whole family in one reply. tenth. free, an access examination and not an order. it concerns two other families, manfred luwinski's of 1965 and joachim leibholz's of 1939, and touches kurt and ivone only at the edges. send when there is time.

and 2 drafts must not be sent. archiwum państwowe w bydgoszczy — asked for the szubin marriage entry of 1874. the document has since been read — bydgoszcz answered on 22 september by pointing at genealogiawarchiwach.pl and the entry was read at the image the same hour: akt nr 9, usc szubin miasto sygn. 141, scan 10. the file is kept rather than deleted, so that nobody writes it again. landesarchiv berlin — two reproductions — asked for two reproductions by exact register number: kurt's 1912 birth entry and the leibholz/luwinski marriage entry. the marriage entry arrived on 29 september, unasked, and the birth entry is now asked for in letter 39 and ordered through the digitaler antrag. it also said kurt left in 1933. the file is kept rather than deleted, so that nobody writes it again.
the address check that did not work rule replaced

this archive’s standing rule was “mx check before sending any email”. on 15 september all twenty-six addresses the project has used were re-resolved and audited against the six that have actually failed. mx caught one of the six.
¦address mx said what happened
¦ahm@mail.exercito.pt no mx caught nxdomain bounce
¦sandfdoc@mweb.co.za live 550 relay access denied
¦enquiries@dac.gov.za live nxdomain, from dsac’s own gateway
¦the same, earlier live department renamed dac → dsac
¦nmphetshwa@justice.gov.za live the person had left the section
¦sandf, visagie street live the office had moved to irene

and here is why a dns check can never catch the commonest failure. dac.gov.za and dsac.gov.za resolve to the same mail gateway. the dead department’s domain keeps a perfectly valid mx record, the shared gateway accepts the mail, and the rejection happens inside, where dns cannot see it.

the replacement, ordered by what actually catches things: search the sent mail first, for prior contact and prior bounces — that has caught three failures; prefer an address the institution itself gave you over one from a directory; check the institution still exists under that name and at that address; then mx, last, to catch a mistyped subdomain; then watch for a bounce for a day.
